version.changelog: 1.1.3: Added Security Disclaimers & Scanner False Positives documentation (Semantic Air-Gapping rationale, Privileged Operations justification). Included Dockerfile in package. 1.1.2: Distroless runtime image (gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12:nonroot).

llm.summary: The skill's code, requirements, and instructions are coherent with a pre-installation sandboxing/inspection tool, but it legitimately needs powerful host capabilities (Docker daemon access, optional root/KVM for micro‑VMs and eBPF) so you should review and run it in an appropriately isolated environment.

dimensions.detail: The name/description (pre-installation sandboxing, 5-layer inspection) matches the included scripts (obfuscator, sandbox orchestrator, eBPF/syscall audit, entropy gate, output filter, postmortem). Required tools (python3, docker) are appropriate. The README explicitly documents optional Firecracker/KVM and eBPF tracing, which explain the need for elevated privileges in advanced modes.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md and scripts instruct the agent to: extract a transcript from the original source, create an obfuscated copy, run that copy in a quarantined runtime (Docker or optional micro-VM), collect output and syscall traces, apply entropy checks and output filtering, and produce a sanitized failure report. All file reads/writes and operations described (reading the provided <source_dir>, building/running containers, writing reports) are consistent with the stated purpose. Note: the tool will read arbitrary code from the supplied source directory and produces an obfuscated copy for execution.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No external install spec is declared (instruction-only), but the SKILL expects you to build a local Docker image from bundled files (bundled Dockerfile) and will pull a runtime image from gcr.io/distroless (a known registry). Building and running the bundled Dockerfile is expected for this tool, but review the Dockerfile before building since it executes locally.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request credentials or env vars, which is appropriate. However, it requires access to the Docker binary/daemon (and optionally root/KVM for Firecracker and eBPF tracing). Access to the Docker daemon or the host kernel (KVM/eBPF) provides broad host-level power in practice; these capabilities are proportionate to kernel-level auditing but materially increase risk if run on a production host or with an untrusted Docker socket. Treat Docker daemon access and KVM/eBPF as sensitive resources.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The registry metadata does not request always:true and the skill does not declare persistent or elevated platform-wide privileges. Autonomous invocation is allowed by default (platform normal). The tool does include optional operations that require root/KVM when chosen, but it does not attempt to modify other skills or system configs beyond orchestrating containers/VMs and producing reports.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
This appears to be a genuine sandboxing/audit tool and its unusual operations (obfuscation, eBPF tracing, micro‑VMs) are explained in the docs. However: 
- Review the bundled Dockerfile and scripts before building/running — the build executes locally. 
- Run Black-Fortress on an isolated host or dedicated VM (not on a shared production box). Docker daemon access (or mounting /var/run/docker.sock) effectively grants host-level control; avoid exposing the Docker socket to untrusted processes. 
- If you do not need micro‑VM/eBPF features, avoid enabling them (they require root/KVM). 
- Verify that pulling the runtime image from gcr.io is acceptable for your environment; you can replace it with an internally vetted image if needed. 
- Understand that the obfuscator creates modified copies of code (originals remain read‑only) — this is intentional to neutralize prompt-injection vectors but also means the executed artifacts differ from the originals. 
- If unsure, test the tool on throwaway code and an isolated test machine first and audit the produced reports and container lifecycles.
